objects.name: Phorpiex Botnet Extortion Activity Monitoring
objects.description:
Summary

IBM X-Force ongoing collection was created to provide you with the latest IoCs and intel on the Phorpiex Botnet Extortion activity found on our environment. The collection will be updated automatically whenever new findings have been determined. Please note that the IoCs within this collection are actionable and hence can be used for blockings to protect your environment. Due to this, it may happen that specific IoCs get removed from the collection in a dynamic time range when no further evidence is available to support the maliciousness of the indicator.

Background

The Phorpiex botnet was initially known as a botnet using the IRC protocol for its operations before switching to a modular architecture. The distribution takes place by exploit kits and through support from other malware families. With this success its operators leverage now operations as Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS). This offering allows other cyber gangs to use the botnet infrastructure for their malicious intentions. However, a big part of its daily threats are the so called "sextortion" spam campaigns. Sextortion in spam campaigns refers to the coercion of victims to pay a certain amount of money within a given time frame under threat of publishing intimate pictures or videos of the victim. This is known to be a fake threat since there is no known case so far where the threat actors proved to posses such material.

Activity Monitor

objects.name: Energy Industry Profile
objects.description:
# Summary

Cyber attacks in the energy industry continue to pose multifaceted risks, spanning economic disruption, safety hazards, and even environmental consequences. Because energy is the backbone of every nation’s critical infrastructure, companies in this sector are especially attractive targets. In all its forms, energy is paramount to the economic stability, national security, and daily functioning of cities and industries.

Recent incidents underscore the threat landscape. In April 2025, Norway's intelligence chief confirmed a [cyberattack on a hydropower dam in Bremanger](https://www.reuters.com/technology/norway-spy-chief-blames-russian-hackers-dam-sabotage-april-2025-08-13/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), where Russian-linked actors briefly seized control over critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, researchers have uncovered [46 new vulnerabilities](https://www.techradar.com/pro/millions-of-solar-power-systems-could-be-at-risk-of-cyber-attacks-after-researchers-find-flurry-of-vulnerabilities?utm_source=chatgpt.com) in major solar inverter brands like Sungrow, Growatt, and SMA, enabling threat actors to manipulate power output, disrupt operations, or steal sensitive data. The industry’s exposure is reflected in its ranking as the fourth-most impacted industry in the [2025 X-Force Threat Intelligence Index](https://www.ibm.com/reports/threat-intelligence), accounting for 11% of attacks across the top ten industries, a figure nearly unchanged from 2024. 

Despite this persistent targeting, the [2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach) shows a modest improvement: the cost to identify and contain a breach fell from 5.29% in 2024 to 4.83% in 2025, representing an 8.7% year-over-year decrease.

Attackers' objectives within the energy sector vary widely. Like other industries, energy companies hold lucrative assets such as customer data, financial information, trade secrets, and proprietary technology. However, the sector is distinguished by its potential for real‑world physical impacts. Operational Technology (OT) systems, including Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) components, are particularly valuable targets for adversaries seeking to monitor or manipulate facility operations. Successful attacks on these systems can severely disrupt the delivery of power, gas, oil, or other essential resources.

IBM X‑Force expects the energy sector to remain a top‑ten target for at least the next three years, with adversaries driven not only by financial incentives but also by geopolitical ambitions and the desire to disrupt critical infrastructure.

# Key Takeaways

**Top Actions on Objectives**

  - Malware - Ransomware, Backdoors, Infostealers
  - Server Access
  - Tool-Credential Acquisition
  - Business Email Compromise (BEC)

**Top Threat Groups**

  - ITG15
  - Hive0103
  - Hive0044
  - Sophisticated ransomware actors

**Top Recommendations**

  - Employ software that can detect and flag suspicious emails
  - Implement multifactor authentication on email and all remote access points
  - Develop and drill a response plan for ransomware that includes recovery from backups
  - Implement a robust patch management program

# Notable Activity and Findings

## IBM X-Force: [The Operational Technology Threat Landscape: Insights from IBM X-Force](https://www.ibm.com/think/x-force/the-operational-technology-threat-landscape-insights-from-x-force)

In September 2025, X-Force released findings on the rising cyber risk to OT environments, highlighting an increasing volume of vulnerabilities, active exploitation, and operational impact. Between January and June 2025, 670 OT-impacting vulnerabilities were disclosed, nearly half rated as high or critical, with 21% of critical flaws having publicly available exploit code. Threat actors continue to exploit perimeter-facing devices such as VPNs, remote gateways, and protocol converters to gain initial access, leveraging vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-32433 (Erlang/OTP SSH), CVE-2025-6543 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2025-0282 (Connect Secure VPN), and CVE-2025-31324 (SAP NetWeaver). IBM reported that 15% of data breach victims experienced OT impact, with average breach costs at $4.56M (above the global average) and nearly a quarter suffering damage to physical systems or equipment. The findings highlight the increasing convergence of IT and OT, the targeting of critical access points, and the need for prioritized patching, segmentation, and tailored threat hunting in critical infrastructure environments.

## IBM X-Force: [Recent Threats from China-aligned Actors](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/e02a23f4-9345-4a30-b506-6e3025c894db)

Over the past two years, China-based threat actor groups, including Volt Typhoon, Salt Typhoon, and Flax Typhoon, have been increasingly active, primarily targeting US critical infrastructure and other global victims. Salt Typhoon, potentially linked to China's Ministry of State Security, specializes in accessing and exploiting vulnerabilities in U.S. telecom networks and sensitive law enforcement systems. Volt Typhoon focuses on prepositioning within US critical infrastructure for future espionage, utilizing LOTL techniques and a Mirai-like botnet. Flax Typhoon, originating from Fuzhou, China, targets strategically important organizations globally, particularly those in Taiwan and countries partnered with Taiwan, exploiting network edge devices for access. These groups are believed to operate as part of China's intelligence gathering efforts, with their activities expected to persist amid rising geopolitical tensions. Each group shares some Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs), yet maintains unique victim focuses and operational strategies.

## OSINT: [Noisy Bear Campaign Targeting Kazakhstan Energy Sector](https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/noisy-bear-targets-kazakhstan-energy.html)

In May 2025, Kazakhstan’s state-owned oil and gas company KazMunaiGas (KMG) was targeted in a phishing campaign attributed to a newly identified threat group “Noisy Bea*r\*\*”*. Threat actors delivered ZIP archives via spear-phishing emails impersonating the internal IT department, containing a malicious LNK downloader, decoy KMG documents, and instructions in Russian and Kazakh. The execution chain deployed a PowerShell loader called DOWNSHELL, ultimately installing a DLL-based implant capable of launching a reverse shell. Infrastructure was hosted on the sanctioned Russian bulletproof provider Aeza Group. While Seqrite Labs assessed the activity as a cyber-espionage operation, KMG stated the emails were part of an internal phishing test conducted in May 2025, raising questions about attribution. The campaign shows the increasing use of localized lures, sanctioned hosting providers, and layered malware delivery techniques against critical energy infrastructure in Central Asia.

## OSINT: [CISA Warning on Oil & Natural Gas Infrastructure](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-hackers-targeting-critical-oil-infrastructure/)

In May 2025, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a warning that unsophisticated threat actors are actively targeting U.S. oil and natural gas infrastructure. Adversaries have been observed attempting to exploit publicly exposed OT devices and human-machine interfaces (HMIs) using default or weak credentials, brute-force attacks, and poorly secured remote access methods. While no confirmed large-scale disruptions have been reported, CISA warned that successful compromises could lead to operational outages, safety risks, environmental damage, and downstream supply chain impact. The advisory urged operators to remove OT systems from the public Internet, enforce strong password policies, secure remote access with phishing-resistant MFA, and segment IT from OT networks. CISA further recommended testing manual fallback processes, disaster recovery plans, and business continuity measures to mitigate potential service interruptions. The persistent risk to critical energy infrastructure was highlighted, where even low-skill actors can now cause significant disruption if poor cyber practices persist.

## OSINT: [Nova Scotia Power Cyberattack](https://therecord.media/thousands-impacted-cyber-nova-scotia)

In March 2025, Nova Scotia Power fell victim to a cyberattack that exposed sensitive data belonging to nearly 280,000 individuals. Threat actors maintained access to internal systems from March 19th to April 25th, exfiltrating customer names, addresses, Social Insurance Numbers, driver’s license data, bank account details, billing history, power consumption records, and other service-related information. The attack forced the company to isolate certain servers and rebuild customer-facing systems, including its phone support line and online MyAccount portal, but power generation and transmission operations were not disrupted. Nova Scotia Power supplies electricity to over 500,000 homes and manages $5 billion in assets and is offering victims two years of credit monitoring services. While the utility has not confirmed ransomware involvement, there was still prolonged down time, sensitive data theft, and operational impact on customer systems.

## IBM X-Force: [HIVE0117 Delivers a Familiar Campaign](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/8c576537-6552-497b-a005-e5b830d8e13a)

In early 2025, X-Force reported that the cybercriminal group Hive0117, also known as DarkWatchman, conducted a significant email campaign targeting Russian speakers. The emails contained a malicious attachment with an enhanced JavaScript backdoor, facilitating the installation of DarkWatchman malware on the recipient's device. Hive0117, active since 2021, has a history of directing phishing campaigns towards individuals linked to key sectors like energy, finance, transport, and software security in Russia, Kazakhstan, Latvia, and Estonia. Their latest tactic involved adding DLL reflection functionality to their malware. Previously, they impersonated Pony Express and the Main Directorate of the Military Commissariat of the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation, respectively, using Russia's mobilization of citizens for their Ukraine conflict and an annual financial reconciliation act as lures. 

# Top Attack Groups

Although security incidents in the energy industry are often not publicly disclosed, several high‑profile events have shed light on common attack sources and methods. According to the [2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach), the average time to detect and contain a breach fell from 277 days to 241 days year over year. While this decline is encouraging, 241 days still represents a significant window in which an attacker can operate inside a network, giving them ample opportunity to study systems, disrupt operations, or exfiltrate or destroy data and equipment.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Nation-State

Nation-state interest in the energy sector and critical infrastructure is of paramount concern to government and security professionals. State-sponsored cyber threat actors act in accordance with various geopolitical agendas have organized extensive cyber warfare campaigns against systems belonging to private companies and foreign governments. State-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups are responsible for the creation of advanced malware which allows them to conduct sophisticated and long running attacks, often against other governments or competing organizations. [Certain APT groups](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-083a) are known to target and infect systems in the energy industry for the purposes of industrial espionage, intellectual property theft, or disruption of service.

### Russian state-sponsored actors

Russian state-sponsored groups have demonstrated repeated and persistent efforts to perform reconnaissance against, compromise, and disrupt the operations of critical infrastructure entities, including those in the energy sector. The majority of these attacks have focused on Ukraine, including attacks on Ukraine's power grid in 2015 and 2016 and similar attempted attacks in 2022. However, Russia has also reportedly performed [years-long reconnaissance](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/fbi-us-energy-sector-faces-reconnaissance-scanning-by-russian-hackers/620863/) campaigns against [critical infrastructure](https://www.us-cert.gov/ncas/alerts/TA18-074A) in the United States, and Russian nationals have [sought to disrupt the operations of energy entities](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/four-russian-government-employees-charged-two-historical-hacking-campaigns-targeting-critical) around the globe on behalf of the Russian government.

Based on repeat observations of Russian cyber operations targeting this sector and enduring state interests, IBM X-Force assesses that these groups will constitute a highly capable and significant threat to energy entities for the foreseeable future.

#### ITG15

Since at least 2011, Russian state-sponsored cyber threat actor [ITG15](https://exchange.xforce.ibmcloud.com/threat-group/guid:22a30b968ce67213af1723a0652fe6b7), which shares campaign overlaps with Dragonfly, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Allanite, Dymalloy, Koala Team, Peace Pipe, and Group 24, has carried out activity against globally distributed targets primarily based in Europe, North America, and Asia Minor. ITG15 campaigns generally focus on industries associated with defense, aviation, critical manufacturing and infrastructure, nuclear technology, and energy. Between March 2016 and March 2018, ITG15 compromised multiple US-based targets associated with Western energy providers, and exfiltrated data specifically associated with ICS and SCADA systems, to include electricity production, transmission and distribution offline.

#### Hive0103

Reported to be active as early as 2009, [Hive0103](https://exchange.xforce.ibmcloud.com/threat-group/guid:85be023f589688341de37d71be99d798) shares campaign overlap with what is tracked in open sources as Sandworm Team, Electrum, Kamacite, VoodooBear, TeleBots, Iron Viking, and Quedagh. The [UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-condemns-russias-gru-over-georgia-cyber-attacks) and [US](https://media.defense.gov/2020/May/28/2002306626/-1/-1/0/CSA%20Sandworm%20Actors%20Exploiting%20Vulnerability%20in%20Exim%20Transfer%20Agent%2020200528.pdf) governments have [attributed](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/six-russian-gru-officers-charged-connection-worldwide-deployment-destructive-malware-and) this activity to Russia’s military Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), specifically its Main Center for Special Technologies (GTsST), field post number 74455. The group has targeted a broad array of industries including energy, government and military, media, sports, transportation, and financial services in Ukraine, Europe, and around the world. Hive0103 operations may have begun as early as 2008 with research pointing to inconclusive [evidence](https://www.secureworks.com/research/blackenergy2) suggesting versions of its main malware toolset at the time were used against Georgian networks coincident with Russian military operations.

In April 2022, it was [reported](https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/04/12/industroyer2-industroyer-reloaded/) that Sandworm, a group that has overlaps with Hive0103, targeted Ukraine's energy sector with so-called 'Industroyer2' malware. Although the attack was ultimately foiled, Sandworm deployed destructive wiper malware to both the company's IT and ICS/OT environments. Industroyer2, which is ICS-capable, was deployed alongside destructive 'CaddyWiper' malware on the ICS network in an attempt to disrupt the power supply (Industroyer2) and wipe traces of the attack (CaddyWiper).

### Chinese state-sponsored actors

Multiple Chinese APT groups have historically been involved in cyber espionage operations against energy and utilities entities. The goal of these groups is to extract confidential information from entities in these sectors, especially in regions of specific interest to the Chinese government. In particular, Chinese state-sponsored operations carrying out cyber economic espionage appear to align with its economic goals, and have targeted entities in areas of economic importance to the Chinese government and other organizations involved in economic developments in the region. IBM tracks one group that has historically been involved in this activity as [Hive0044](https://exchange.xforce.ibmcloud.com/threat-group/guid:73c0b973d8db578fc30e3232f1e3f00a), which overlaps with APT15.

## Cybercriminals

### Sophisticated Ransomware Actors

Many of the most sophisticated ransomware actors today operate under the Ransomware-as-a-Service model, where ransomware developers contract out to highly-skilled affiliates the delivery of the ransomware to victims, and then take a portion of the proceeds once a ransom is paid. In addition, many groups also steal sensitive victim data before encrypting files and then threaten to release or sell stolen data if a ransom is not paid. This “double extortion” tactic places added pressure on a victim to pay—even if they are able to successfully and independently recover from the ransomware attack. A handful of ransomware groups also use “triple extortion” tactics, further threatening to carry out DDoS attacks on the victim if a ransom is not paid. In December 2024, it was reported that [Electrica](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/romanian-energy-supplier-electrica-hit-by-ransomware-attack/), a Romanian energy supplier was victim to Lynx ransomware. Fortunately the company's SCADA systems were not impacted by this attack, likely due to proper network segmentation.

### Hive0118

[Hive0118](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/13619ea3-9ee5-4ed7-9c58-67d2bf824f9a) (aka TA577 aka TR aka Tramp) is an initial access broker and email distributor known for delivering Qakbot and later Pikabot malware. In the months following the Qakbot disruption in summer 2023,TA577 also delivered IcedID and DarkGate malware, before settling in Pikabot. TA577 campaigns have featured the use of several crypters related to ITG23 and ITG26, including Oracle, Dave, Quicksand, Snow, and Forest. TA577 in particular has a close relationship with the Qakbot group (ITG26) and has been a prolific Qakbot distributor, but X-Force also assess ties to former ITG23 members as well.

### Hive0133

[Hive0133](https://opencti.intsum.ibm.com/dashboard/analyses/reports/0fb940f4-577f-4241-b58c-63e0a2a1b77a) is an initial access broker and email distributor that overlaps with the group TA544. They are most well known for their association with the Cutwail botnet and delivering Gozi and later WailingCrab malware. The group has also delivered other malware, including IcedID. This distributor also has a relationship with ITG23 and has delivered malware using ITG23 crypters. Hive0133 is most well-known for targeting organizations in Italy, but over the past year they have expanded their targeting to include organizations worldwide.

### Hive0138

Hive0138 is an email spammer that X-Force has been tracking since at September 2023. This spammer's campaigns are less frequent than other tracked spammers, with campaigns taking place every 1-4weeks on average. Hive0138 has delivered Bumblebee, DarkGate, ParallaxRAT, Forest-crypted Sliver, and Botyara. The majority of their campaigns have resulted in either Bumblebee or Sliver payloads.

# Top Actions on Objectives

X‑Force classifies “actions on objectives” based on what the attacker was doing at the point in the attack lifecycle when X‑Force was brought in to respond. This view does not always represent the attacker’s ultimate goal, which could include data exfiltration, ransomware deployment, espionage, or other outcomes. In 2024, the most common action on objective observed by X‑Force in the energy sector was malware deployment, accounting for 24% of all incidents. This was followed by the malicious use of legitimate IT tools, server access, and business email compromise, each representing 8% of incidents. Further details can be found in the [X-Force Threat Intelligence Index](https://www.ibm.com/reports/threat-intelligence). 

# Risk Mitigation Measures

**Ransomware:** Develop and drill a response plan for ransomware that includes restoring a network from backups and encrypting data to make it less profitable if stolen. Defense-in-depth and endpoint detection solutions can assist in identifying ransomware attackers before they deploy malware on a system. For additional information on countering ransomware attacks, see IBM's [The Definitive Guide to Ransomware](https://www.ibm.com/think/x-force/ransomware-renaissance-definitive-guide-2023).

**Phishing:** There are several steps organizations can take to combat this threat. Employ software that can detect and flag suspicious e-mails. Disable macros, email delegates, and mail forwarding. Routinely provide employee education with updated phishing techniques used by attackers. Warn employees to beware of e-mails that create a sense of urgency. Make it very easy for employees to report phishing e-mails, as early alerts can warn others in a company.

**Vulnerability exploitation:**  Implement a robust patch management solution that focuses on vulnerabilities that are most relevant to your environment and includes a testing platform to assess the effect of patches and remediation measures in your network. Identify potential cybersecurity weaknesses in medical devices by implementing testing throughout the development process, possibly using penetration testing to audit security compliance and effectiveness.

**BEC:** While BEC attacks have been common over the past two years, X-Force incident response data suggests that BEC attacks are decreasing. X-Force assesses that organizations’ successful implementation of multifactor authentication (MFA) is a significant contributor to this downward trend. Employ MFA to make it much more difficult for threat actors to use guessed or stolen credentials to get into a network.

Cyber attacks in the energy industry continue to pose multifaceted risks, spanning economic disruption, safety hazards, and even environmental consequences. Because energy is the backbone of every nation’s critical infrastructure, companies in this sector are especially attractive targets. In all its forms, energy is paramount to the economic stability, national security, and daily functioning of cities and industries.

Recent incidents underscore the threat landscape. In April 2025, Norway's intelligence chief confirmed a [cyberattack on a hydropower dam in Bremanger](https://www.reuters.com/technology/norway-spy-chief-blames-russian-hackers-dam-sabotage-april-2025-08-13/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), where Russian-linked actors briefly seized control over critical infrastructure. Meanwhile, researchers have uncovered [46 new vulnerabilities](https://www.techradar.com/pro/millions-of-solar-power-systems-could-be-at-risk-of-cyber-attacks-after-researchers-find-flurry-of-vulnerabilities?utm_source=chatgpt.com) in major solar inverter brands like Sungrow, Growatt, and SMA, enabling threat actors to manipulate power output, disrupt operations, or steal sensitive data. The industry’s exposure is reflected in its ranking as the fourth-most impacted industry in the [2025 X-Force Threat Intelligence Index](https://www.ibm.com/reports/threat-intelligence), accounting for 11% of attacks across the top ten industries, a figure nearly unchanged from 2024. 

Despite this persistent targeting, the [2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach) shows a modest improvement: the cost to identify and contain a breach fell from 5.29% in 2024 to 4.83% in 2025, representing an 8.7% year-over-year decrease.

However, the sector is distinguished by its potential for real‑world physical impacts. Operational Technology (OT) systems, including Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) components, are particularly valuable targets for adversaries seeking to monitor or manipulate facility operations. Successful attacks on these systems can severely disrupt the delivery of power, gas, oil, or other essential resources.

IBM X‑Force expects the energy sector to remain a top‑ten target for at least the next three years, with adversaries driven not only by financial incentives but also by geopolitical ambitions and the desire to disrupt critical infrastructure.

objects.name: IBM X-Force Reports Intelligence Extensions
objects.description: This schema extends the Reports STIX object to include additional IBM X-Force Report Intelligence properties.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Dataease: Redshift JDBC RCE Bypass
objects.description: Dataease is an open source data visualization analysis tool. Prior to 2.10.20, By controlling the IniFile parameter, an attacker can force the JDBC driver to load an attacker-controlled configuration file. This configuration file can inject dangerous JDBC properties, leading to remote code execution.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Local File Inclusion in Contact Plan, E-Mail, SMS and Fax components in Asseco SEE Live 2.0
objects.description: Local File Inclusion in Contact Plan, E-Mail, SMS and Fax components in Asseco SEE Live 2.0 allows remote authenticated users to access files on the host via "path" parameter in the downloadAttachment and downloadAttachmentFromPath API calls.

objects.name: Hive0162 adds Threadveil to their Repertoire
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: IBM X-Force has been tracking clusters of likely-related activity since August 2025. In December, X-Force observed a similar cluster of activity featuring a new Hijackloader component, "Threadveil", used as a second-stage loader. This activity aligns with previous observations, where the ultimate goal is the delivering of the commodity RAT DCRat. After analyzing all clusters of activity, and noting comparable tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), it is highly likely that all clusters of activity are related, in which X-Force is defining as a LATAM-originating hive, Hive0162.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for OneUptime: Password Reset Token Logged at INFO Level
objects.description: OneUptime is a solution for monitoring and managing online services. Prior to 10.0.24, the password reset flow logs the complete password reset URL — containing the plaintext reset token — at INFO log level, which is enabled by default in production. Anyone with access to application logs (log aggregation, Docker logs, Kubernetes pod logs) can intercept reset tokens and perform account takeover on any user.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for undici is vulnerable to CRLF Injection via upgrade option
objects.description:
When an application passes user-controlled input to the upgrade option of client.request(), an attacker can inject CRLF sequences (
) to inject arbitrary HTTP headers or terminate the HTTP request prematurely and smuggle raw data to non-HTTP services.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Cap'n Proto has an integer overflow in KJ-HTTP
objects.description: Cap'n Proto is a data interchange format and capability-based RPC system. Prior to 1.4.0, a negative Content-Length value was converted to unsigned, treating it as an impossibly large length instead. In theory, this bug could enable HTTP request/response smuggling.

objects.name: CabinetRAT Analysis Report (INT00017846)
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description:
CabinetRAT is a backdoor used in a campaign attributed to the threat group UAC-0245, which may relate to UAC-0184/Hive0156.

The infection chain starts with a ZIP file containing an XLL file. When a user executes the file, Microsoft Excel loads it as a plugin, causing it to execute the *xlAutoOpen*export function, which stores the malicious code.

Before executing the actual backdoor, the malware first drops its other components: another XLL file (loader.xll), an EXE file (runner.exe), and a PNG file. The executable file's purpose is to stealthily launch Microsoft Excel. Launching Excel in this manner loads the XLL file, which then finds the shellcode stored in the PNG file. The malware executes the shellcode in memory, which acts as the actual backdoor.

CabinetRAT uses multiple anti-virtualization and anti-debugging techniques to avoid detection. It also employs string obfuscation and on-the-fly API resolving.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Unhead has a Bypass of URI Scheme Sanitization in makeTagSafe via Case-Sensitivity
objects.description: Unhead is a document head and template manager. Prior to 2.1.11, The link.href check in makeTagSafe (safe.ts) uses String.includes(), which is case-sensitive. Browsers treat URI schemes case-insensitively. DATA:text/css,... is the same as data:text/css,... to the browser, but 'DATA:...'.includes('data:') returns false. An attacker can inject arbitrary CSS for UI redressing or data exfiltration via CSS attribute selectors with background-image callbacks. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.1.11.

objects.name: IP Report for IP address 158.94.209.120
objects.description: One of the five RIRs announced a (new) location mapping of the IP.

objects.name: CHAR Backdoor Malware Family Profile
objects.x_com_ibm_short_description: CHAR is a simple Rust-based backdoor implemented as a Telegram bot using the open-source Teloxide library. The malware supports a short list of bot commands, such as changing the current directory and executing commands via cmd.exe or PowerShell.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for @backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend: Possible exposure of defaultEnvironment secrets using dry-run endpoint
objects.description: Authenticated users with permission to execute scaffolder dry-runs can gain access to server-configured environment secrets through the dry-run API response. Secrets are properly redacted in log output but not in all parts of the response payload.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Inspektor Gadget: Tracing Denial of Service via Event Flooding
objects.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. Prior to 0.50.1, in a situation where the ring-buffer of a gadget is – incidentally or maliciously – already full, the gadget will silently drop events. The include/gadget/buffer.h file contains definitions for the Buffer API that gadgets can use to, among the other things, transfer data from eBPF programs to userspace. For hosts running a modern enough Linux kernel (>= 5.8), this transfer mechanism is based on ring-buffers. The size of the ring-buffer for the gadgets is hard-coded to 256KB. When a gadget_reserve_buf fails because of insufficient space, the gadget silently cleans up without producing an alert. The lost count reported by the eBPF operator, when using ring-buffers – the modern choice – is hardcoded to zero. The vulnerability can be used by a malicious event source (e.g. a compromised container) to cause a Denial Of Service, forcing the system to drop events coming from other containers (or the same container). This vulnerability is fixed in 0.50.1.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Dataease: Unfiltered active SVG content leads to Stored XSS
objects.description: Dataease is an open source data visualization analysis tool. In DataEase 2.10.19 and earlier, the static resource upload interface allows SVG uploads. However, backend validation only checks whether the XML is parseable and whether the root node is svg. It does not sanitize active content such as onload/onerror event handlers or script-capable attributes. As a result, an attacker can upload a malicious SVG and then trigger script execution in a browser by visiting the exposed static resource URL, forming a full stored XSS exploitation chain.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for A vulnerability allowing an authenticated domain user to perform remote code execution (RCE) on the Backup Server.
objects.description: A vulnerability allowing an authenticated domain user to perform remote code execution (RCE) on the Backup Server.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Stack Buffer Overflow in HMS Networks Ewon Flexy and Cosy+
objects.description: HMS Networks Ewon Flexy with firmware before 15.0s4, Cosy+ with firmware 22.xx before 22.1s6, and Cosy+ with firmware 23.xx before 23.0s3 have a stack buffer overflow that leads to a Denial of Service, which can also be exploited to achieve Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge
objects.description: A Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm vulnerability in Trane Tracer SC, Tracer SC+, and Tracer Concierge could allow an attacker to bypass authentication and gain root-level access to the device.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Trane has released the following versions of Tracer SC+ for users to upgrade to: CVE-2026-28252: Tracer SC+ version v6.30.2313

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Parse Server OAuth2 adapter shares mutable state across providers via singleton instance
objects.description: Parse Server is an open source backend that can be deployed to any infrastructure that can run Node.js. Prior to 9.6.0-alpha.11 and 8.6.37, Parse Server's built-in OAuth2 auth adapter exports a singleton instance that is reused directly across all OAuth2 provider configurations. Under concurrent authentication requests for different OAuth2 providers, one provider's token validation may execute using another provider's configuration, potentially allowing a token that should be rejected by one provider to be accepted because it is validated against a different provider's policy. Deployments that configure multiple OAuth2 providers via the oauth2: true flag are affected.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for ZeptoClaw: Generic webhook channel trusts caller-supplied identity fields; allowlist is checked against untrusted payload data
objects.description: ZeptoClaw is a personal AI assistant. Prior to 0.7.6, the generic webhook channel trusts caller-supplied identity fields (sender, chat_id) from the request body and applies authorization checks to those untrusted values. Because authentication is optional and defaults to disabled (auth_token: None), an attacker who can reach POST /webhook can spoof an allowlisted sender and choose arbitrary chat_id values, enabling high-risk message spoofing and potential IDOR-style session/chat routing abuse.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Local Privilege Escalation on Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication Servers
objects.description: A vulnerability allowing local privilege escalation on Windows-based Veeam Backup & Replication servers.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for swag/platform-security: `/api/_info/config` route exposes information about licenses and active security fixes
objects.description: Shopware is an open commerce platform. /api/_info/config route exposes information about active security fixes.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Tenda i12 wifiSSIDget formwrlSSIDget stack-based overflow
objects.description: A security vulnerability has been detected in Tenda i12 1.0.0.6(2204). The impacted element is the function formwrlSSIDget of the file /goform/wifiSSIDget. Such manipulation of the argument index leads to stack-based buffer overflow. The attack may be launched remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Stack buffer overflow vulnerability in D-Link DIR-513 v1.10
objects.description: Stack buffer overflow vulnerability in D-Link DIR-513 v1.10 via the curTime parameter to goform/formSetWizardSelectMode.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by insufficient policy enforcement in DevTools. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Google Chrome security bypass
objects.description: Google Chrome could allow a remote attacker to bypass security restrictions, caused by insufficient policy enforcement in PDF. By persuading a victim to visit a specially crafted Web site, an attacker could exploit this vulnerability to bypass security restrictions.
objects.x_xfe_remedy: Upgrade to the latest version of Google Chrome (146.0.7680.71 or 146.0.7680.72 or later), available from the Google Chrome Releases Web site. See References.

objects.name: Vulnerability Report for Tenda i12 exeCommand vos_strcpy stack-based overflow
objects.description: A security flaw has been discovered in Tenda i12 1.0.0.6(2204). Impacted is the function vos_strcpy of the file /goform/exeCommand. The manipulation of the argument cmdinput results in stack-based buffer overflow. The attack can be launched remotely.
